Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive power in the base and exponent is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes the origin; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L:\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L:L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: Fix the inertial frame and chart $x$ of the given data; by [L1] one has $D=E^{-1}(q-p)$, and in the $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the interval of the pair is $\eta(q-p,q-p)=-(D^0)^2+|D_s|^2$ in the notation of [L2].

Since $q-p$ is spacelike, [L3] gives $\eta(q-p,q-p)>0$, so $-(D^0)^2+|D_s|^2>0$, that is $(D^0)^2<|D_s|^2$; hence $D_s\ne 0$ and $e:=D_s/|D_s|$ is a well-defined unit spatial vector, the quotient $c:=D^0/|D_s|$ satisfies $|c|<1$ and is an admissible boost parameter, and $(c+1)/2$ and $(c-1)/2$ also lie in $(-1,1)$.

Fix a real number $b$ with $|b|<1$, put $\beta:=be$, $B_b:=B(\beta)$ and $e'_a:=B_b^{-1}e_a=B(-\beta)e_a$ for $a=0,1,2,3$. By [L5] and [L6] the map $B_b^{-1}=B(-\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, so $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an $\eta$-orthonormal, future, positively oriented ordered basis of $V$, hence $(o;e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an inertial frame of the model by [L1]. Writing $x_b$ for its chart, $M_b$ for the matrix of $B_b$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $E_b(u):=\sum_a u^a e'_a$, one has $E_b(u)=B_b^{-1}(E(u))$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^4$ by linearity of $B_b^{-1}$, hence $E_b^{-1}=E^{-1}B_b$ and $x_b(r)=E_b^{-1}(r-o)=E^{-1}(B_b(r-o))=E^{-1}(B_b(E(x(r))))=M_b\,x(r)$ for every $r\in A$, because $r-o=E(x(r))$ and $E^{-1}B_bE$ is the matrix map $u\mapsto M_bu$.

By linearity of $B_b$, subtracting the chart identity of step 3.1 at $p$ from the identity at $q$ gives $x_b(q)-x_b(p)=M_bD$, and its time component is $(M_bD)^0=\gamma_b(D^0-b|D_s|)$, where $\gamma_b:=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}>0$: the first row of $M_b$ gives $(M_bD)^0=\gamma_b(D^0-\beta\cdot D)$, and $\beta\cdot D=b\,(e\cdot D_s)=b|D_s|$ by [L8]. Since $D^0=c|D_s|$, this reads $x_b^0(q)-x_b^0(p)=\gamma_b|D_s|(c-b)$, which is positive for $b<c$, zero for $b=c$ and negative for $b>c$; moreover each matrix entry of $M_b$, namely $\gamma_b$, $-\gamma_b b\,e_i$ and $\delta^i_j+(\gamma_b-1)e_ie_j$, is a continuous function of $b$ on $(-1,1)$, because $b\mapsto\gamma_b$ is continuous and positive there with $\gamma_b\to 1$ as $b\to 0$, so every coordinate $x_b^a(r)$ is continuous in $b$.
The frame of step 3.1 with parameter $b:=c$, admissible by step 2.1, has chart $x_0:=x_c$ satisfying $x_0^0(q)-x_0^0(p)=0$ by step 4.1; this is assertion (b).

The frames of step 3.1 with parameters $b_+:=(c-1)/2$ and $b_-:=(c+1)/2$, both admissible by step 2.1, have $x_{b_+}^0(q)-x_{b_+}^0(p)=\gamma_{b_+}|D_s|(c-b_+)>0$ and $x_{b_-}^0(q)-x_{b_-}^0(p)=\gamma_{b_-}|D_s|(c-b_-)<0$ by step 4.1, since $c-b_+=(c+1)/2>0>c-b_-=(c-1)/2$; taking $x_+:=x_{b_+}$ and $x_-:=x_{b_-}$ this is assertion (c).

Assertion (a) is step 2.1 read in an arbitrary inertial chart; assertion (d) is the construction of steps 3.1 and 4.1, comprising the chart identity $x_b=B(be)\circ x$, the time-difference formula, the sign trichotomy relative to $c=D^0/|D_s|$ and the continuous dependence on $b$; assertions (b) and (c) are steps 5.1 and 5.2. Only inertial charts of the model and one explicitly constructed basis per parameter are used, "simultaneous" is the equality of the frame's $x^0$ coordinate as required in (e), and no choice principle is used since each parameter is a single explicit real number.

citations.quote:
Let $x : [a,b] \to A$, $a < b$, be a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve in the sense of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], with a finite partition
$a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, $C^{1}$ on each open piece and finite one-sided
difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of each piece. Assume its tangents
are nonzero future causal at every open-piece point and at each one-sided
endpoint.

In any inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) write
$y = (y^{0},z)$, $z \in \mathbb{R}^{3}$, for the coordinate path. On a piece
$(\alpha,\beta)$, choose $r \in (\alpha,\beta)$; for a function $g$ continuous
there, write

$$\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} g \;:=\; \lim_{u \downarrow \alpha} \int_u^{r} g \;+\; \lim_{v \uparrow \beta} \int_r^{v} g$$

when both limits are finite. Then:

**(a)** $y$ is continuous on $[\alpha,\beta]$, $y^{0'} \ge |z'| \ge 0$ on
$(\alpha,\beta)$, and $y^{0'} > 0$ there.

**(b)** Every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable
(its absolute value has finite improper integral), and its signed improper
integral equals the corresponding endpoint increment. The continuous functions
$|z'|$ and $f = \sqrt{(y^{0'})^{2} - |z'|^{2}} = \sqrt{-\eta(x',x')}$ have
finite nonnegative improper integrals, with
$\int_{(\alpha,\beta)} f \le \int_{(\alpha,\beta)} y^{0'} = y^{0}(\beta) - y^{0}(\alpha)$.

**(c)** The improper values are independent of $r$, additive under subdivision,
and the finite piece sums are independent of the admissible partition.

**(d)** $D = x(b)-x(a)$ is nonzero future causal: $D^{0} > 0$ and
$|D_{\mathrm{spatial}}| \le D^{0}$ in every inertial chart. If some interior or
one-sided endpoint tangent is future timelike, then $D$ is future timelike.
Coordinate time is strictly increasing on every nondegenerate subinterval. The
integrals need not be ordinary closed-piece Riemann integrals. No
derivative-limit hypothesis, Lebesgue-integration premise, clock identification,
or choice principle is used.

Let $c > 0$ be the conversion constant of [[def-sr-proper-time]] and let
$x : [a,b] \to A$, $a < b$, be a piecewise $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline in
the weak sense of [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]: $x$ is $C^{1}$
on each open piece of a finite partition $a = s_0 < \cdots < s_m = b$, its
interior tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient endpoint tangents are
future timelike, and continuous extension of the derivative is not assumed.

**(i) The piecewise density.** On each open piece let

$$g_i(t) = \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(t),x'(t)\bigr)} > 0 .$$

By clause (b) of [[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]] the function
$g_i$ is continuous on $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and its two-ended improper Riemann
integral

$$\int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} g_i \;:=\; \lim_{u \downarrow s_{i-1}} \int_u^{r} g_i \;+\; \lim_{v \uparrow s_i} \int_r^{v} g_i$$

(for any $r \in (s_{i-1},s_i)$) is finite and nonnegative; it is positive
because $g_i$ is positive and continuous on a nondegenerate compact interior
subinterval, the improper value dominates the ordinary integral over such a
subinterval ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]), and that ordinary integral
is strictly positive: a continuous nonnegative function on a nondegenerate
compact interval whose integral vanishes is identically zero there
([[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]), whereas $g_i$ is
strictly positive at every point of the piece.

**(ii) Total proper time.** Define

$$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) \;:=\; c^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \int_{(s_{i-1},s_i)} g_i .$$

The finite sum is independent of the admissible partition, by subdivision
additivity and a common refinement (clause (c) of
[[lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability]]), and it is independent of the
inertial chart: for every truncation $s_{i-1} < u < r < v < s_i$ the ordinary
integral $\int_u^v g_i$ is intrinsic by [[def-sr-proper-time]] (applied to the
$C^{1}$ restriction), and the improper value is the limit of these intrinsic
truncation values, which is intrinsic.

**(iii) Based proper-time function.** For a distinguished $s_0 \in [a,b]$ set
$\tau_x(s) := \Delta\tau_{[s_0,s]}(x)$ for $s \ge s_0$ and
$\tau_x(s) := -\Delta\tau_{[s,s_0]}(x)$ for $s < s_0$, with
$\tau_x(s_0) = 0$, using restrictions and oriented limits
([[def-oriented-integral]], [[def-interval]]). It is strictly increasing, and
changing the distinguished base point changes it by an additive constant.

**(iv) Corner hypothesis (H).** Hypothesis (H) is the special case in which
each open-piece derivative has finite limits at both ends of its piece and hence
extends continuously to the closed piece. Under (H) the limiting values equal
the finite one-sided quotient derivatives of the curve, each $g_i$ extends
continuously and positively to the closed piece, its improper integral equals
its ordinary Riemann integral there
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[thm-ftc-second-part]]), and the same
finite-sum formula applies. In particular, if $x$ is globally $C^{1}$ on
$[a,b]$ (the one-piece case of (H)), then
$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = \tau(b) - \tau(a)$ of [[def-sr-proper-time]].

**(v) Straight pieces.** If on the piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the tangent is a
constant future timelike vector $d_i$, the contribution of that piece is
$c^{-1}(s_i - s_{i-1})\sqrt{-\eta(d_i,d_i)}$; a piecewise straight future
timelike worldline therefore has total proper time equal to the finite sum of
its straight-segment proper times. In every case $\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) > 0$.

**(vi) Additivity over concatenation.** For $a < d < b$, the restrictions of a
weak piecewise worldline $x$ to $[a,d]$ and $[d,b]$ satisfy
$\Delta\tau_{[a,b]}(x) = \Delta\tau_{[a,d]}(x) + \Delta\tau_{[d,b]}(x)$: insert
$d$ into the partition and use (ii).

The definition supplies metric time only; identification with an ideal clock
reading is a separate physical assumption. No global $C^{1}$ inverse, tangent at
a kink, or four-acceleration at a kink is asserted.

Let $c > 0$ be a fixed real number, the conversion constant of the model, and
let $x : I \to A$ be a $C^{1}$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]).

**The integrand.** The function

$$g_x : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad g_x(s) := -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr),$$

is continuous and strictly positive. For continuity, fix an inertial frame and
write $y := x_A \circ x$ for the coordinate path; by clause (a) of
[[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]] the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$y'$ is continuous, so each component $y'^{a}$, $a \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, is a
continuous real function ([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]). In the
$\eta$-orthonormal basis underlying the frame one has
$\eta(e_a,e_b) = \operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), whence

$$g_x(s) = -\eta\bigl(x'(s),x'(s)\bigr) = \bigl(y'^{0}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{1}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{2}(s)\bigr)^{2} - \bigl(y'^{3}(s)\bigr)^{2},$$

a finite sum of products of continuous real functions, hence continuous
([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]],
[[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]). Strict positivity
$g_x(s) = -\eta(x'(s),x'(s)) > 0$ is exactly the future timelike hypothesis on
$x'(s)$ ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]).

**The proper-time function.** Hence $u \mapsto \sqrt{g_x(u)}$ is continuous on
$I$: the square root is the power $t^{1/2}$ of [[def-rational-power]], which is
continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$
([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]), and it is composed with the
continuous positive function $g_x$
([[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); consequently it is Riemann
integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[def-interval]]). For $s_0, s \in I$
the **proper time from $s_0$ to $s$** is

$$\tau(s) := c^{-1} \int_{s_0}^{s} \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

the integral being taken with oriented limits as in [[def-oriented-integral]];
for $a < b$ in $I$ this reads

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \int_a^b \sqrt{-\eta\bigl(x'(u),x'(u)\bigr)}\; du,$$

which on a compact interval containing $a$ and $s_0$ is the value at $b$ of the
integral function with base point $a$ of the integrand
([[def-the-integral-function]]). Changing the base point $s_0$ changes $\tau$
by an additive constant, so the elapsed times between parameter values are
intrinsic. $\tau$ depends on the parametrized history $x$ and on the parameter
values; its invariance under increasing $C^{1}$ reparametrizations is proved in
[[lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance]].

**Straight segments.** For the straight future timelike segment
$x(s) = p + (s-s_0)(q-p)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] the difference
quotients are identically the future timelike displacement $q-p$, so
$x'(s) = q-p$ and

$$\tau(b) - \tau(a) = c^{-1} \sqrt{-\eta(q-p,q-p)}\,(b-a),$$

the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions.

**Scope.** The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a
null point the integrand vanishes, so the integral is constant; for a spacelike
curve $-\eta(x',x')$ is negative and the square root is not a real number; and
for a past-directed timelike curve the same integral is defined but is not
attached to a worldline of this model. The construction asserts nothing about
physical clock readings.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and use
the reachability objects $J^+$, $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$$
be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part $v_s:=v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ of a
vector $v=v^0e_0+v_s$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then:

**(a) Cone description.** $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$,
$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; moreover every $v\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$v\ne 0$ satisfies $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$, and $v$ is future
null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$.

**(b) Finite sums.** If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ lie in $\overline{C^+}$
($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

**(c) Coordinate criterion.** For events $p,q\in A$ put
$D^a:=x^a(q)-x^a(p)$ and $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$. Then: $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only
if $D^0\ge|D_s|$; $q\in I^+(p)$ if and only if $D^0>|D_s|$; $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ if and only if $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$; and for $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ one has $0<D^0$ and $|D_s|\le D^0$. The criteria are stated for the
chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is
$\eta$-orthonormal with future first vector.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed
time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to $\le$, $J^+$ or $I^+$ and
uses no choice principle.

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]): $A$ is a nonempty affine space over
the $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ with displacement vectors $q-p$ and
translations $v \mapsto p+v$ ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]), and $C^+$
is one of the two connected components of the timelike set
$T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, chosen as the time orientation, with
$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ the other component
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$\overline{C^+}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and
$\overline{C^-}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ for the future and past closed cones.
A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal according to the sign
of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is
not causal, and the causal vectors are exactly the nonzero elements of
$\overline{C^+}\cup\overline{C^-}$.

**The closed cones and their boundaries.** By
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], applied in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$, the closure of the
component $\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ of the timelike set is
$\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ with boundary points exactly $0$ and the nonzero null
vectors of $\overline{C^+}$. Writing $N^+$ and $N^-$ for the sets of nonzero
future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

**The objects fixed by this definition.**

**(a) Causal and chronological reachability.** For events $p,q\in A$ set
$p\le q$ if and only if $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$, and $p<q$ if and only if
$q-p\in C^+$. The first relation is read "$q$ is causally reachable from $p$"
and the second "$q$ is strictly (chronologically) reachable from $p$"; both are
relations on the set of events, and neither is asserted here to have any
property beyond being a relation.

**(b) Futures and pasts.** For an event $p\in A$ set

$$J^+(p):=\{q\in A:p\le q\}=p+\overline{C^+},\qquad I^+(p):=\{q\in A:p<q\}=p+C^+,$$

$$J^-(p):=\{q\in A:q\le p\}=p+\overline{C^-},\qquad I^-(p):=\{q\in A:q<p\}=p+C^-.$$

The displayed equalities hold because $q\in J^+(p)$ says exactly that the
displacement $q-p$ lies in $\overline{C^+}$, that is $q=p+v$ for some
$v\in\overline{C^+}$; here $p+v$ is the affine translation of
[[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]. Since $0\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}$
one has $p\in J^+(p)\cap J^-(p)$, and since $0$ is not timelike one has
$p\notin I^+(p)$ and $p\notin I^-(p)$. The sets
$J^\pm(p)$ and $I^\pm(p)$ are called the causal and chronological future and
past of $p$.

**(c) Causal diamonds.** For events $p,q\in A$ with $p\le q$, the causal diamond
of the ordered pair $(p,q)$ is the set

$$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)=\{r\in A:p\le r\le q\}.$$

The diamond is defined only under the hypothesis $p\le q$; some of its
properties are computed in the examples page of this pair.

**(d) Reachability by future causal paths.** A piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path is a piecewise $C^1$ curve $x:[a,b]\to A$ on a compact interval with
$a<b$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) all of
whose tangents are future causal: at every interior point of every open smooth
piece the tangent $x'(s)$ exists and is future causal, and at every partition
point of $[a,b]$ and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ both one-sided
difference-quotient tangents that exist there exist and are future causal
vectors in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. For events $p,q\in A$, say
that $q$ is reachable from $p$ by a future causal path when $p=q$, or when
$p\ne q$ and there are real numbers $a<b$ and a piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path $x:[a,b]\to A$ with $x(a)=p$ and $x(b)=q$. Write $R^+(p)$ for the set of
events reachable from $p$ in this sense; thus $p\in R^+(p)$ by the first clause.

**(e) Conventions and scope.** All objects above are defined from the affine
structure of $A$, the form $\eta$ and the time orientation alone: no chart, no
choice of origin, no spatial orientation of $V$ and no unit convention enters
their definition. This item asserts no property of these objects
beyond their being well-defined sets and relations: the reflexivity of $\le$ is
part of (b), while the transitivity of $\le$, the identification
$R^+(p)=J^+(p)$, the antisymmetry "$p\le q$ and $q\le p$ imply $p=q$", the
monotonicity of inertial coordinate time along future causal paths and the
invariance of these objects under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps are
proved later on this page and are not used here. No choice principle is used:
all objects are subsets or finite data built from a finite-dimensional real
vector space.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^{+})$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $I$ be an order-convex subset of
$\mathbb{R}$ with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]); a **curve** of the
model is a map $x : I \to A$.

### Derivative and regularity of the parametrization

For $s \in I$ and $h \ne 0$ with $s+h \in I$ the **difference quotient**
$\bigl(x(s+h)-x(s)\bigr)/h$ is an element of $V$, the displacement from $x(s)$
to $x(s+h)$ divided by the real number $h$
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). Convergence in $V$ is understood through
an inertial frame: for the frame isomorphism $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ of an
inertial frame ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) put
$|v|_{E} := |E^{-1}v|_{2}$, the Euclidean norm transported by $E$. If $E'$ is
the isomorphism of another inertial frame, then $E'^{-1}E$ and its inverse are
linear maps $\mathbb{R}^{4} \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$, so they are bounded with
constants $K, K' \ge 0$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]):
$|v|_{E'} \le K'\,|v|_{E}$ and $|v|_{E} \le K\,|v|_{E'}$ for all $v \in V$.
The two transported norms are therefore equivalent, give the same limits, and
give the same notion of differentiability. The curve is **differentiable at
$s$** when the limit of the difference quotients as $h \to 0$ (over
$h \ne 0$, $s+h \in I$; one-sided at the endpoints of $I$) exists in $V$; then
this limit, written $x'(s) \in V$, is the **tangent vector** of $x$ at $s$, and
it does not depend on the inertial frame used to describe the convergence.

If $x_A : A \to \mathbb{R}^{4}$ is the global chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], [[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]),
then $x$ is differentiable at $s$ exactly when the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map
$x_A \circ x$ is differentiable at $s$ in the sense of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], because $E^{-1}$ is linear and
carries the difference quotients of $x$ to those of $x_A \circ x$; and then

$$x'(s) = E\bigl((x_A \circ x)'(s)\bigr),$$

where $E : \mathbb{R}^{4} \to V$ is the frame isomorphism
$E(u) = \sum_{a} u^{a} e_{a}$. This value does not depend on the inertial chart
used: two inertial charts are related by an affine bijection with an invertible
linear part ([[lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas]]), the chain
rule transports the coordinate derivative accordingly, and all norms on the
finite-dimensional space $V$ give the same limit.

The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

### Causal character

Let $x$ be differentiable at $s \in I$. Then $x$ is **regular at $s$** if
$x'(s) \ne 0$; $x$ is **timelike** (respectively **null**, **spacelike**,
**causal**) **at $s$** if the vector $x'(s)$ is timelike (respectively null,
spacelike, causal) in the sense of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and $x$ is
**future-directed at $s$** if $x'(s)$ is future timelike or future null in the
sense of [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. The zero vector has
no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at $s$.

### Worldlines

A **future timelike worldline** (equivalently, a **massive worldline**) is a
$C^{1}$ curve $x : I \to A$ with $x'(s)$ future timelike for every $s \in I$; a
**future causal curve** (respectively a **future null curve**) is a $C^{1}$
curve with $x'(s)$ future causal (respectively future null) for every
$s \in I$. A **piecewise $C^{1}$ worldline** is a piecewise $C^{1}$ curve whose
tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided
difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future
timelike; a **$C^{k}$ worldline** is a worldline whose parametrization is
$C^{k}$. $C^{2}$ regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]] available.

The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike
worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve $s \mapsto x(-s)$, which
is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to
it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by
an explicit formula.

Let $V$ be a real vector space, with addition $+$, zero $0$, and additive
inverses ([[def-vector-space]]). An **affine space over $V$** is a nonempty set
$A$ together with a map

$$+\;:\;A\times V\longrightarrow A,\qquad (p,v)\longmapsto p+v,$$

such that

1. $(p+v)+w=p+(v+w)$ and $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$ and $v,w\in V$; and
2. for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$.

The map in clause 1 is the **action** of $V$ on $A$. The unique vector supplied
by clause 2 is written $q-p$ and is called the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**;
thus $q-p$ is the unique $v\in V$ with $p+v=q$. An affine space over the real
vector space $V$ is also called a **real affine space modelled on $V$**, and
then $V$ is its **space of displacements**.

The following identities are consequences of the two clauses, with the displayed
justification:

- $p+(q-p)=q$ for all $p,q\in A$: this restates the defining property of $q-p$
  in clause 2.
- $p-p=0$ for all $p\in A$: taking $q=p$ in the previous display gives
  $p+(p-p)=p=p+0$, and clause 2 applied to the pair $(p,p)$ gives
  $p-p=0$.
- $p+0=p$ for all $p\in A$: this is clause 1.
- $(q-p)+(r-q)=r-p$ for all $p,q,r\in A$:
  $p+\bigl[(q-p)+(r-q)\bigr]=\bigl[p+(q-p)\bigr]+(r-q)=q+(r-q)=r=p+(r-p)$,
  so clause 2 applied to the pair $(p,r)$ identifies the two vectors.
- For each $p\in A$ the map $v\mapsto p+v$ is a bijection of $A$ with $V$: it is
  surjective by clause 2 applied to $q:=p+v$, and injective because
  $p+v=p+w$ gives $p+(v-w)=\bigl[p+v\bigr]+(-w)=p+w-w=p=p+0$, so clause 2
  applied to $(p,p)$ gives $v-w=0$, that is, $v=w$.

**Affine coordinate systems.** Suppose $V$ is $4$-dimensional and
$E:\mathbb R^4\to V$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]).
For a chosen point $o\in A$, define

$$x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),\qquad p\in A .$$

This is a bijection $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$: it is injective and surjective because
$E^{-1}$ is a bijection and $p\mapsto p-o$ is a bijection of $A$ with $V$ by the
bijection just proved, applied with that $o$. Such maps are the **affine
coordinate systems on $A$**; clause 2 is exactly what makes them well defined,
because it is clause 2 that attaches to each ordered pair $(o,p)$ a unique
displacement $p-o$.

An **oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space** is a quadruple
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ consisting of the following four pieces of data.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

The following terminology is attached to such a quadruple.

- The elements $p$ of $A$ are the **events**; for events $p,q$ the vector
  $q-p\in V$ is the **displacement from $p$ to $q$**.
- The **interval** of $p,q\in A$ is the real number
  $I(p,q):=\eta(q-p,q-p)=q(q-p)$.
- Events $p,q$ are **timelike**, **null**, **spacelike** or **causally
  related** when the displacement $q-p$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal
  in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; they are
  **future-related** when $q-p$ is future causal and **past-related** when
  $q-p$ is past causal in the sense of
  [[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**No point of $A$ is distinguished.** For every $v\in V$ the translation
$\tau_v:A\to A$, $\tau_v(p):=p+v$, is a bijection, since it is inverse to
$\tau_{-v}$: $\tau_{-v}(\tau_v(p))=(p+v)+(-v)=p+(v-v)=p$ and symmetrically, by
the affine action axioms ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). Displacements
are translation invariant, $\tau_v(q)-\tau_v(p)=q-p$, so every $\tau_v$ preserves
the interval, the causal classification of every ordered pair, and the sets
$C^+$, $C^-$ (which are subsets of $V$, independent of the point of $A$); it
changes only the labelling of points. The mathematical structure of the model is
exactly the quadruple $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$; no derived physical quantity (proper
time, four-velocity, momentum, energy, charge or any field) is part of this
definition, and all later structure of the framework (frames, charts, tensor
fields, worldlines) is built on this model.

**Well-definedness.** The affine-space definition supplies the action and the
unique displacements; the Lorentz-form definition supplies $\eta$ and its
inertia; the determinant-line definition supplies orientations; and the two
components of $T$ between which the time-orientation definition chooses exist by
the components lemma recorded in the well-definedness clause of
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]], which is also what makes the
names future and past causal in item 4 well defined.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
