2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive power in the base and exponent is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes the origin; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

**Why this item is first.** The published definition of the integral does not
cover this page. [[def-darboux-integral]] is stated for reals $a < b$, because
the partitions it quantifies over are those of [[def-partition-and-refinement]],
whose standing hypothesis is $a < b$: with $a = b$ the chain
$a = t_0 < \dots < t_n = b$ is unsatisfiable. So $\int_a^b f$ is an undefined
symbol whenever $a \ge b$, and every additivity statement below would be
ill-formed as it is usually written. This item extends the notation, and nothing
else: the object it names is still the Darboux integral of
[[def-darboux-integral]].

Let $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ and write

$$[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v] \;:=\; \text{the closed interval with endpoints } u \text{ and } v$$

([[def-interval]]). Let $f$ be a real-valued function whose domain contains that
interval. Say that **$f$ is integrable between $u$ and $v$** when either $u = v$,
or $u \ne v$ and the restriction of $f$ to $[u \wedge v,\ u \vee v]$ is bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable there ([[def-darboux-integral]],
[[def-darboux-sums]]). For such $f$ define

$$\int_u^v f \;:=\; \begin{cases} \text{the Darboux integral of } f \text{ over } [u,v] & \text{if } u < v, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } u = v, \\[2pt] -\displaystyle\int_v^u f & \text{if } u > v. \end{cases}$$

**There is nothing to check for consistency.** The three clauses are indexed by
the three cases of trichotomy, $u < v$, $u = v$ and $u > v$, which are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive; no pair of them ever applies to the same $(u,v)$. In
particular the first clause is untouched, so on $u < v$ this is the published
integral verbatim and every published theorem about it applies unchanged.

**The middle clause is a stipulation, not a computation.** It is *not* claimed
that $0$ is a value forced by the $u < v$ definition in any limiting sense; that
definition simply says nothing at $u = v$, and $\int_u^u f := 0$ is what is
written there. It is also unconditional: no hypothesis on $f$ beyond being
defined at $u$ is asked for, since the case $u = v$ never refers to a partition.

### The two consequences used throughout the page

**Antisymmetry, for every pair.** For all reals $u, v$ with $f$ integrable
between them,

$$\int_u^v f \;=\; -\int_v^u f .$$

Indeed if $u < v$ then $v > u$ and the third clause reads
$\int_v^u f = -\int_u^v f$, which rearranges to the display; if $u = v$ both
sides are $0$; and if $u > v$ the third clause is the display itself.

**Absolute values agree.** Consequently
$\bigl|\int_u^v f\bigr| = \bigl|\int_v^u f\bigr|$ for every such pair.

**An obligation recorded here and discharged elsewhere.** With this convention
the additivity identity

$$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f$$

holds for **every** arrangement of $u, v, w$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable, not only for $u < v < w$. That is a theorem and not part of this
definition; it is proved as the last clause of
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], and nothing on this page uses it before it
is proved there.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]) with $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ and

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; 0 .$$

Then $f(x) = 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$.

**This is the exact repair of a published false statement.** Without continuity
the conclusion fails: [[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]],
on the companion page of *The Riemann Integral*, exhibits a nonnegative
integrable function with integral $0$ that is positive at every rational point.
The remark there says that the continuous case is true and that its proof was
not available at that point in the reading order, because additivity over
subintervals had not been proved. It is proved now
([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]), and this item is that proof.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$

derivations.claim: Let $a<b$ and let $x:[a,b]\to A$ be a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path with $D=x(b)-x(a)$, and fix an inertial chart, writing $\mathrm{x}=(\mathrm{x}^0,z)$ for the coordinate path of $x$; by [L6] the coordinate path is piecewise $C^1$ with the same partition and with one-sided tangents $\mathrm{x}'=E^{-1}x'$, which are nonzero future causal because $x'$ is and $E^{-1}$ is linear with the coordinate criterion of [L3] read in this basis. If some one-sided tangent of $x$ is future timelike, [L1] gives $D$ future timelike, that is $D\in C^+$ by [L3]. In particular $D\ne0$ for every such path with $a<b$, so the third clause of (a) holds; this is (a).

otin C^+$ by [L4], and $p$ is not in the first or third set because the straight path from $p$ to $p$ has the constant tangent $0$, which is not future timelike, and a path from $p$ to itself with a future timelike tangent cannot exist as just shown.

For (d): let $[a',b']\subseteq[a,b]$ and let $y$ be a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path; the restriction $y|_{[a',b']}$ is again a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path (its tangents are tangents of $y$, or absent when $a'=b'$), so step 1.1 gives $D':=y(b')-y(a')\in\overline{C^+}$; writing $\mathrm{y}$ for the coordinate path of $y$ in the chart $x$, one has $(\mathrm{x}^0\circ y)(b')-(\mathrm{x}^0\circ y)(a')=D'^0$ by [L6], and $D'^0\ge|D'_s|\ge0$ by [L3]; hence $x^0\circ y$ is nondecreasing. If $y$ is nonconstant on $[a',b']$ then $y|_{[a',b']}$ is nonconstant, so step 1.1 gives $D'\ne0$, and a nonzero element of $\overline{C^+}$ has positive time coordinate by [L3], that is $(\mathrm{x}^0\circ y)(b')>(\mathrm{x}^0\circ y)(a')$; this is (d).

For (c): if $p\le q$ and $q\le p$ then $D=q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ and $p-q=-D\in\overline{C^+}$, so $D\in\overline{C^-}=-\overline{C^+}$ and $D\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$ by [L3], that is $p=q$. Conversely, if antisymmetry fails, that is $p
e q$ with $p\le q$ and $q\le p$, then step 2.1 makes the straight paths from $p$ to $q$ and from $q$ to $p$ future causal, and their concatenation $z:[0,2]	o A$, $z(s)=p+s(q-p)$ for $s\in[0,1]$ and $z(s)=q+(s-1)(p-q)$ for $s\in[1,2]$, is a closed piecewise $C^1$ future causal path with $z(0)=z(2)=p$ and $z(1)=q
e p$; conversely, if a nonconstant closed piecewise $C^1$ future causal path $x:[a,b]	o A$ with $x(b)=x(a)=p$ exists, choose $s\in(a,b)$ with $x(s)
e p$, which exists because $x$ is nonconstant on $[a,b]$ and $x(a)=x(b)$; applying step 1.1 to the restrictions to $[a,s]$ and $[s,b]$ gives $x(s)-p\in\overline{C^+}$ and $p-x(s)\in\overline{C^+}$, that is $p\le x(s)$ and $x(s)\le p$ with $x(s)
e p$, so antisymmetry fails. Hence the antisymmetry of $\le$ is equivalent to the absence of a nonconstant closed piecewise $C^1$ future causal path; this is (c).

For (e), normalization: since $q\in I^+(p)$, step 2.2 says the straight path from $p$ to $q$ is future timelike; in particular $D=q-p$ is a future timelike vector, so $\eta(D,D)<0$ and $T=\sqrt{-\eta(D,D)}>0$, and $D\in C^+$ by [L4]. Choose the inertial frame with origin event $p$, so that $x(p)=0$ and the coordinates of $D$ in this frame are those of $x(q)$. The vector $v:=D/T$ satisfies $\eta(v,v)=\eta(D,D)/T^2=-1$ and $v\in C^+$ (a positive multiple of a future timelike vector), so $v$ is future unit timelike; write $v=(v^0,v_{\mathrm{vec}})$ in coordinates, so that $v^0>0$, $|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|<v^0$ and $(v^0)^2-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2=1$ by [L3] and [L5]. Put $\beta:=v_{\mathrm{vec}}/v^0$; then $|\beta|<1$ and $B:=B(\beta)$ is proper orthochronous by [L7], so $Bv$ is future unit timelike, and its time coordinate is $\gamma(v^0-\beta\cdot v_{\mathrm{vec}})=\gamma\bigl((v^0)^2-|v_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2\bigr)/v^0=\gamma/v^0$ with $\gamma=(1-|\beta|^2)^{-1/2}=v^0$; hence $(Bv)^0=1$, and since $\eta(Bv,Bv)=-1$ the spatial part of $Bv$ satisfies $|(Bv)_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2=((Bv)^0)^2-1=0$ by [L5], so $Bv=e_0$ and $BD=T\,e_0$. The ordered basis $e'_a:=B^{-1}e_a$ is $\eta$-orthonormal, future and positively oriented because $B^{-1}$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and such maps preserve $\eta$, the cone $C^+$, the orientation and the volume form by [L7] and [L8], so $(p;e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an inertial frame; its chart $x_1$ satisfies $x_1=B\circ x$ (same origin $p$), because with $E_1(u)=\sum_a u^ae'_a=B^{-1}\bigl(E(u)\bigr)$ one has $E_1^{-1}=E^{-1}B$ and $x_1(r)=E_1^{-1}(r-p)=E^{-1}\bigl(B(r-p)\bigr)=E^{-1}\bigl(B(E(x(r)))\bigr)=M_Bx(r)$ for the matrix $M_B$ of $B$ by [L8] and [L6]; therefore $x_1(q)-x_1(p)=BD=T\,e_0$, with coordinates $(T,0,0,0)$.

For (f): let $F$ be a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map, so $F(r)=F(p_0)+L(r-p_0)$ with $L$ a linear Lorentz map, and $F(r+v)=F(r)+Lv$ for all $r\in A$ and $v\in V$ by [L8]. For a piecewise $C^1$ curve $z:[a,b]\to A$ the composition $F\circ z$ is piecewise $C^1$ on the same partition with $(F\circ z)'=L\circ z'$: the difference quotients satisfy $\bigl(F(z(s+h))-F(z(s))\bigr)/h=L\bigl((z(s+h)-z(s))/h\bigr)$, and $L$ is continuous and linear, so the limit is $L(z'(s))$ by [L6] and [L8]. Since $L$ and $L^{-1}$ preserve the causal character of every nonzero vector and the cone $C^+$ by [L8], the composition $F\circ z$ is a future causal path, respectively a future timelike path, exactly when $z$ is; with the definition of $R^+$ in [L4] this gives $F(R^+(p))=R^+(F(p))$, and with $J^+=R^+$ from step 2.1 it gives $F(J^+(p))=J^+(F(p))$. For the chronological future, $q\in I^+(p)$ iff the straight path from $p$ to $q$ is future timelike by step 2.2; its image under $F$ is the straight path from $F(p)$ to $F(q)$ with constant tangent $L(q-p)$ by [L6], and $L(q-p)$ is future timelike exactly when $q-p$ is by [L8], so $F(I^+(p))=I^+(F(p))$ (the reverse inclusion follows by applying the same argument to $F^{-1}$, which is again a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map). Finally $F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)$, so $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ iff $L(q-p)\in\overline{C^+}$ by the cone preservation, that is $p\le q$ iff $F(p)\le F(q)$; this is (f).

For the inequality of (e): let $y:[a,b]\to A$ be a piecewise $C^1$ future timelike worldline with $y(a)=p$ and $y(b)=q$, with weak pieces $a=a_1<b_1=\dots<b_m=b$, and let $y_1:=x_1\circ y$ be its coordinate path in the chart $x_1$ of step 3.2. By [L6] and the affinity of $x_1$ from step 3.2, $y_1$ is piecewise $C^1$ on the same partition with tangents $y_1'=B\,y'$, and these are future timelike because $y'$ is and $B$ preserves $\eta$ and the cone by [L8]; writing $y_1=(y_1^0,z_1)$ with spatial part $z_1$, [L3] gives $y_1^{0'}\ge|z_1'|\ge0$ and $y_1^{0'}>0$ on each open piece. For such numbers $0\le|z_1'|\le y_1^{0'}$ one has $\sqrt{(y_1^{0'})^2-|z_1'|^2}\le y_1^{0'}$ with equality exactly when $z_1'=0$. Applying [L1] to the coordinate path $y_1$ on each piece $(a_i,b_i)$ gives finite nonnegative improper integrals with $\int_{(a_i,b_i)}\sqrt{(y_1^{0'})^2-|z_1'|^2}\le\int_{(a_i,b_i)}y_1^{0'}=y_1^0(b_i)-y_1^0(a_i)$, and summing over the finitely many pieces [L2] and telescoping across the continuous junctions give $c\,\Delta\tau(y)=\sum_i\int_{(a_i,b_i)}\sqrt{(y_1^{0'})^2-|z_1'|^2}\le y_1^0(b)-y_1^0(a)=x_1^0(q)-x_1^0(p)=T$, because $x_1(q)-x_1(p)=(T,0,0,0)$ by step 3.2; hence $\Delta\tau(y)\le T/c$.

For the equality case of (e): $\Delta\tau(y)=T/c$ holds exactly when equality holds in every piece of step 4.1, that is when $\int_{(a_i,b_i)}h_i=0$ for the nonnegative continuous function $h_i:=y_1^{0'}-\sqrt{(y_1^{0'})^2-|z_1'|^2}$ on each open piece. If $h_i(s_0)>0$ at some point of an open piece, continuity gives a compact subinterval $[u,v]$ of that piece on which $h_i\ge h_i(s_0)/2>0$, so the improper integral dominates the proper integral over $[u,v]$ and is at least $h_i(s_0)(v-u)/2>0$ by [L9], a contradiction; hence $h_i\equiv0$ and $z_1'=0$ on each open piece. By [L10] each spatial coordinate of $y_1$ is constant on each open piece, and by continuity of $y_1$ the spatial coordinates are constant on all of $[a,b]$; since $x_1(p)=0$ and $x_1(q)=(T,0,0,0)$, the constant is $0$, so $y_1(s)=(\sigma(s),0,0,0)$ for the continuous function $\sigma:=y_1^0$ on $[a,b]$, which is $C^1$ on each open piece with $\sigma'=y_1^{0'}>0$; for $s<t$ in $[a,b]$ the increment $\sigma(t)-\sigma(s)$ is the sum of the increments $\sigma(\min(t,s_k))-\sigma(\max(s,s_{k-1}))$ over the finitely many pieces meeting $[s,t]$, each summand is nonnegative by [L11] applied on the closed piece (both arguments lie in that closed piece, where $\sigma$ is continuous, and $\sigma'>0$ on its interior), and at least one summand is strictly positive because its two arguments differ as $s<t$; hence $\sigma$ is strictly increasing, with $\sigma(a)=0$ and $\sigma(b)=T$. Therefore $y(s)=x_1^{-1}(\sigma(s),0,0,0)=p+\frac{\sigma(s)}{T}D$ by [L6], that is $y$ is the strictly increasing reparametrization $s\mapsto p+\varphi(s)D$ of the straight segment from $p$ to $q$, where $\varphi:=\sigma/T$ is a continuous strictly increasing surjection $[a,b]\to[0,1]$, $C^1$ on the open pieces with $\varphi'>0$. Conversely, if $y(s)=p+\varphi(s)D$ with such a $\varphi$, then $y'=\varphi'D$ on each open piece, so $\eta(y',y')=\varphi'^2\eta(D,D)=-(\varphi'T)^2$ and the density is $\varphi'T$; hence $c\,\Delta\tau(y)=T\sum_i\int_{(a_i,b_i)}\varphi'=T\sum_i\bigl(\varphi(b_i)-\varphi(a_i)\bigr)=T\bigl(\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\bigr)=T$ by [L2] and [L9], giving $\Delta\tau(y)=T/c$ exactly for the strictly increasing reparametrizations of the straight segment: this is the equality case of (e). Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and use
the reachability objects $J^+$, $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$$
be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part $v_s:=v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ of a
vector $v=v^0e_0+v_s$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then:

**(a) Cone description.** $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$,
$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; moreover every $v\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$v\ne 0$ satisfies $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$, and $v$ is future
null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$.

**(b) Finite sums.** If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ lie in $\overline{C^+}$
($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

**(c) Coordinate criterion.** For events $p,q\in A$ put
$D^a:=x^a(q)-x^a(p)$ and $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$. Then: $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only
if $D^0\ge|D_s|$; $q\in I^+(p)$ if and only if $D^0>|D_s|$; $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ if and only if $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$; and for $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ one has $0<D^0$ and $|D_s|\le D^0$. The criteria are stated for the
chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is
$\eta$-orthonormal with future first vector.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed
time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to $\le$, $J^+$ or $I^+$ and
uses no choice principle.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $p,q\in A$ with $p\ne q$ and $q-p$
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Then:

**(a)** In the chart $x$ of every inertial frame the coordinate differences
$D:=x(q)-x(p)$ satisfy $|D^0|<|D_s|$, where $|D_s|$ is the Euclidean norm of the
spatial part $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$ of $D$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); in particular
$D_s\ne 0$.

**(b)** There is an inertial frame whose chart $x_0$ satisfies
$x_0^0(q)=x_0^0(p)$: the two events are simultaneous in that frame.

**(c)** There are inertial frames whose charts $x_+$ and $x_-$ satisfy
$x_+^0(q)>x_+^0(p)$ and $x_-^0(q)<x_-^0(p)$.

**(d) Explicit family.** Fix an inertial frame with chart $x$ and let
$e:=D_s/|D_s|$, so that $e$ is a unit spatial vector of that frame. For every
real number $b$ with $|b|<1$ let $B(be)$ be the passive boost of
[[def-lorentz-boost]] with parameter $be$, and let $x_b$ be the chart of the
inertial frame whose ordered basis is $e'_a:=B(be)^{-1}e_a$ and whose origin
event is the same event $o$. Then $x_b=B(be)\circ x$ (the linear map acting on
coordinate columns) and
$$x_b^0(q)-x_b^0(p)=\gamma_b\bigl(D^0-b|D_s|\bigr),\qquad \gamma_b:=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}.$$
This number is positive for $b<D^0/|D_s|$, zero for $b=D^0/|D_s|$ and negative
for $b>D^0/|D_s|$; since $-1<D^0/|D_s|<1$ by (a), all three cases occur among
values $|b|<1$, and the family $b\mapsto x_b$ depends continuously on $b$.

**(e) Scope.** The lemma concerns the inertial charts of the model;
"simultaneous in the frame" means equality of the frame's time coordinate
$x^0$, and no synchronization procedure, observer convention or physical
identification is asserted. No choice principle is used.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with
the reachability objects $\le$, $<$, $J^+$, $I^+$ and $R^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]].

**(a) Displacement of a future causal path.** Let $a<b$ be real numbers and let
$x:[a,b]\to A$ be a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path with $D:=x(b)-x(a)$. Then
$D\in\overline{C^+}$. If $x$ has a future timelike one-sided tangent at some
point of $[a,b]$, then $D\in C^+$. If $x$ is nonconstant, then $D\ne 0$.

**(b) Reachability and straight segments.** $J^+(p)=R^+(p)$, and for $q\ne p$
one has $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only if the straight path
$s\mapsto p+s(q-p)$, $s\in[0,1]$, is a future causal path; moreover
$$I^+(p)=\{q:\text{the straight path from }p\text{ to }q\text{ is future timelike}\} =\{q:q\text{ is reachable from }p\text{ by a piecewise }C^1\text{ future causal path having a future timelike one-sided tangent at some point}\},$$
and $p$ is in neither of these two sets.

**(c) No causal loops.** If $p\le q$ and $q\le p$ then $p=q$; equivalently
there is no nonconstant piecewise $C^1$ future causal path $x:[a,b]\to A$ with
$x(b)=x(a)$.

**(d) Time monotonicity.** For the chart $x$ of every inertial frame and every
piecewise $C^1$ future causal path $y:[a,b]\to A$, the composition $x^0\circ y$
is nondecreasing, and if $y$ is nonconstant on a subinterval $[a',b']$ of
$[a,b]$ then $(x^0\circ y)(b')>(x^0\circ y)(a')$; in particular every inertial
frame agrees that a nonconstant future causal path does not go backwards in
coordinate time.

**(e) Straight-worldline maximum.** Let $p,q$ be events with $q\in I^+(p)$, put
$D:=q-p$ and $T:=\sqrt{-\eta(D,D)}>0$. Then for every piecewise $C^1$ future
timelike worldline $y:[a,b]\to A$ with $y(a)=p$ and $y(b)=q$, the elapsed
proper time
$$\Delta\tau(y)=c^{-1}\sum_i\int_{(a_i,b_i)}\sqrt{-\eta(y',y')},$$
defined by the finite improper-piece sum of
[[def-sr-piecewise-proper-time]] on the weak $C^1$ pieces
$a=a_1<b_1=a_2<\dots<b_m=b$, is at most $T/c$; equality holds if and only if
the image of $y$ is the straight segment from $p$ to $q$ and $y$ traverses it
with a strictly increasing time coordinate, that is, $y$ is a strictly
increasing reparametrization of $s\mapsto p+sD$.

**(f) Invariance.** For every proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map $F$ of the
model one has $F(J^+(p))=J^+(F(p))$ and $F(I^+(p))=I^+(F(p))$ for every event
$p$, and $p\le q$ if and only if $F(p)\le F(q)$ for all events $p,q$.

**(g) Scope.** The theorem concerns the affine model: it attaches no physical
interpretation to $\le$, $J^+$, $I^+$ and $R^+$, asserts nothing about partial
differential equations, propagation of particular fields or differentiability
beyond piecewise $C^1$, and uses no choice principle.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Adopt the postulates of the spacetime-primitives page: the oriented
time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ as the spacetime of the
framework with the equations of the specified model covariant under proper
orthochronous affine Lorentz maps, which are the inertial changes of
description ([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]), and the ideal clock and ideal
light assumptions, including that ideal vacuum light rays are the future null
straight lines and that inertial charts use $x^0=ct$
([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]). Let $x$ and $x'$ be the
charts of any two inertial frames of the model. Then:

(i) the transition $x'\circ x^{-1}$ is an affine map $u\mapsto\Lambda u+b$
whose linear part $\Lambda$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix; in
particular for all events $p,q$ with coordinate differences
$\Delta=x(q)-x(p)$ and $\Delta'=x'(q)-x'(p)$ one has $\Delta'=\Lambda\Delta$
and $\eta_0(\Delta',\Delta')=\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$, where
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: the interval computed from the
coordinates of two events does not depend on the inertial chart used;

(ii) the causal classification of the displacement $q-p$ (timelike, null or
spacelike) and, for causal displacements, the relation "$q$ is in the future
of $p$" versus "$q$ is in the past of $p$" are independent of the inertial
chart used to compute them; likewise the sign of the interval
$I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)$ is chart-independent;

(iii) the class of future null straight lines is preserved by every inertial
transition: if a curve is a future null straight line in one inertial chart,
then its coordinate image in every other inertial chart is again a future null
straight line, and its coordinate speed computed as
$|\Delta x|/\Delta t$ equals $c$ in every inertial chart, consistently with
the light clause of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]];

(iv) the orientation and the oriented volume form of the model are invariant
under every inertial transition, and the composition of two inertial
transitions is again an inertial transition; for two transitions whose
relative parameters are $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ in a common spatial direction
the composed parameter is
$(\beta_1+\beta_2)/(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$.

**Scope and qualification.** This is a conditional statement about the adopted
model with ideal clocks, ideal light rays, flat classical spacetime and no
gravitational or quantum effects. It is not an empirical claim about nature,
it does not derive the postulates from experiment or from verbal symmetry
principles, and it inherits the idealizations of its premises; no measurement,
calibration or statistical inference is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L:\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L:L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following restriction on
signal transmission, called the **causal signal restriction of the model**.

**(i) Causal restriction.** Let $p$ and $q$ be the emission and reception
events of an idealized transmission that carries a signal, where a *signal* is
understood as information, or a physical marker by which a prepared operation
at the emission event is correlated with an observation at the reception event,
within the model. Then the model admits such a transmission only if $q$ lies in
the causal future $J^+(p)$ of $p$
([[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]), that is, only if
the displacement $q-p$ is zero or future causal
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); equivalently, no signal
connects an event with an event outside its closed future light cone.

**(ii) Ideal light.** The ideal vacuum light signals of
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] are the null boundary case of the
restriction: their displacement between emission and reception is future null,
so in the chart of every inertial frame with $x^0=ct$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]) they attain
$|x_s(q)-x_s(p)|=x^0(q)-x^0(p)$.

**(iii) Status.** This is an adopted assumption about the idealized model; it is
not a theorem of the affine geometry of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], it is
not derived here from the other postulates or from any experiment, and it is not
an empirical claim about nature. In particular the framework does not assert
that no physical process whatsoever exceeds $c$, and the question whether any
specified physical process is a signal of this model, and with what reliability
and reach, is left to a separate experimental interface.

**(iv) Explicit non-restriction.** The assumption does not forbid kinematic
patterns in which spacelike-separated events are produced by independent
prearranged mechanisms without any signal or energy transfer between them (for
example a prearranged row of devices triggered in a fixed sequence), and it
imposes no bound on correlations between spacelike-separated events.

**(v) Scope.** The assumption concerns idealized point-like transmission events
in the flat classical model and carries no statistical, apparatus, source or
detector content; no choice principle is used.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

Adopt the assumption that the equations of the specific mechanical and
electromagnetic models developed from this framework are covariant under the
inertial changes of description: each such model equation has the same form
when its events are relabelled by $F$ and its displacements and other tensors
are transformed by $L$.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$

derivations.claim: Clause (i). Suppose a signal is transmitted from $p$ to $q$. By [L1] the model admits this only if $q\in J^+(p)$. If $q\ne p$, then $D=q-p$ is a nonzero element of $\overline{C^+}$, so $D^0>0$ and $D^0\ge|D_s|$ by [L2]; in the chart $x$ of any inertial frame, $D^0=x^0(q)-x^0(p)$ and $|D_s|=|x_s(q)-x_s(p)|$ by the affine linearity of the chart, so $x^0(q)>x^0(p)$ and $|x_s(q)-x_s(p)|\le x^0(q)-x^0(p)$. Since the chart is arbitrary and the computation used the same criterion available in every inertial chart, every inertial frame's time order places the reception after the emission, and the temporal order of the endpoints of the transmission is the same in every inertial frame.

Clause (ii). Let signals be transmitted from $p$ to $q$ and from $q$ to $r$. By [L1] applied twice, $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ and $r-q\in\overline{C^+}$, so $r-p=(q-p)+(r-q)\in\overline{C^+}$ by the finite-sums clause of [L2], that is $r\in J^+(p)$. If in addition $q\in I^+(p)$, that is $q-p\in C^+$, or $r\in I^+(q)$, that is $r-q\in C^+$, the strict case of the same clause gives $r-p\in C^+$, that is $r\in I^+(p)$. In particular a relay whose second leg is causal does not leave the causal future of the first emission, and if either leg has nonzero displacement then its time-coordinate increment is positive, while the other increment is nonnegative by [L2], so the total increment is positive and the relay cannot return to the first emission event.

Clause (iii). If signals are transmitted from $p$ to $q$ and from $q$ to $p$, then [L1] gives $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$ and $p-q\in\overline{C^+}$; by the antisymmetry clause of [L4] (equivalently by $\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$ from [L2]) this forces $q-p=0$, that is $p=q$. For a finite chain $p_0\to p_1\to\cdots\to p_n$, every leg displacement lies in $\overline{C^+}$ by [L1], so every inertial time-coordinate increment is nonnegative, and is strictly positive if that leg displacement is nonzero by [L2]. If the chain is closed, telescoping gives total time-coordinate increment zero; a finite sum of nonnegative reals is zero only when every summand is zero, and [L2] then forces every displacement to be zero. Conversely, if every displacement is zero then $p_0=p_1=\cdots=p_n$, so the chain is closed. Thus only the all-zero chains are closed, and no nontrivial chain returns to its own emission event.

Clause (iv). By the covariance clause of [L4] one has $F(J^+(p))=J^+(F(p))$, $F(I^+(p))=I^+(F(p))$ and $p\le q$ iff $F(p)\le F(q)$ for every proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map $F$, and by [L5] these maps are exactly the inertial changes of description of the model. Since [L1] admits a signal from $p$ to $q$ only when $q\in J^+(p)$, the condition is preserved under every change of description; [L6] records independently that the causal classification and the future/past alternative of the specified model are chart independent, in agreement with [[pthm-sr-interval-and-cone-invariance]].

Clause (v). Let $q-p$ be spacelike. By the first clause of [L3], $|D^0|<|D_s|$ in every inertial chart, so neither $D^0\ge|D_s|$ nor $-D^0\ge|D_s|$ holds; by [L2] $q

otin J^-(p)$, and by [L1] no signal is transmitted from $p$ to $q$ (nor from $q$ to $p$). By the remaining clauses of [L3] there are inertial frames whose charts assign $x^0(q)-x^0(p)$ either sign, including zero. Conversely, if the temporal order of a pair $p
e q$ is observer-independent with the emission $p$ the earlier endpoint, then the displacement is not spacelike by [L3], hence it is nonzero causal by the classification clauses of [L6], and since $p$ is the earlier endpoint the displacement lies in $\overline{C^+}$; the model's restriction admits a transmission only in the future direction by [L1], so the restriction is exactly the requirement that transmissions occur only between events whose temporal order is observer-independent, with the emission the earlier endpoint.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and use
the reachability objects $J^+$, $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$$
be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part $v_s:=v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ of a
vector $v=v^0e_0+v_s$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then:

**(a) Cone description.** $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$,
$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; moreover every $v\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$v\ne 0$ satisfies $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$, and $v$ is future
null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$.

**(b) Finite sums.** If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ lie in $\overline{C^+}$
($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

**(c) Coordinate criterion.** For events $p,q\in A$ put
$D^a:=x^a(q)-x^a(p)$ and $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$. Then: $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only
if $D^0\ge|D_s|$; $q\in I^+(p)$ if and only if $D^0>|D_s|$; $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ if and only if $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$; and for $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ one has $0<D^0$ and $|D_s|\le D^0$. The criteria are stated for the
chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is
$\eta$-orthonormal with future first vector.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed
time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to $\le$, $J^+$ or $I^+$ and
uses no choice principle.

- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
