citations.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) and use
the reachability objects $J^+$, $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]. Let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with chart $x$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) and let
$$|v_s|:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}$$
be the Euclidean norm of the spatial part $v_s:=v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ of a
vector $v=v^0e_0+v_s$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Then:

**(a) Cone description.** $C^+=\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$,
$\overline{C^+}=\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$, $C^-=\{v:-v^0>|v_s|\}$ and
$\overline{C^-}=\{v:-v^0\ge|v_s|\}$; moreover every $v\in\overline{C^+}$ with
$v\ne 0$ satisfies $-\eta(v,e_0)=v^0>0$ and $|v_s|\le v^0$, and $v$ is future
null exactly when $|v_s|=v^0>0$.

**(b) Finite sums.** If $v_1,\dots,v_k$ lie in $\overline{C^+}$
($k\ge 1$), then $v_1+\cdots+v_k\in\overline{C^+}$; if in addition at least one
$v_i$ lies in $C^+$, then the sum lies in $C^+$; and if $v+w=0$ with
$v,w\in\overline{C^+}$, then $v=w=0$.

**(c) Coordinate criterion.** For events $p,q\in A$ put
$D^a:=x^a(q)-x^a(p)$ and $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$. Then: $q\in J^+(p)$ if and only
if $D^0\ge|D_s|$; $q\in I^+(p)$ if and only if $D^0>|D_s|$; $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ if and only if $D^0\ge|D_s|$ and $D^0>0$; and for $q\in J^+(p)$ with
$q\ne p$ one has $0<D^0$ and $|D_s|\le D^0$. The criteria are stated for the
chart of any inertial frame, because every inertial basis is
$\eta$-orthonormal with future first vector.

**(d) Scope.** The lemma is a statement about the affine model and the fixed
time orientation; it attaches no physical meaning to $\le$, $J^+$ or $I^+$ and
uses no choice principle.

Throughout, $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ is an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]): $A$ is a nonempty affine space over
the $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ with displacement vectors $q-p$ and
translations $v \mapsto p+v$ ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]), and $C^+$
is one of the two connected components of the timelike set
$T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, chosen as the time orientation, with
$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ the other component
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]). Write
$\overline{C^+}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and
$\overline{C^-}:=\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ for the future and past closed cones.
A vector $v\in V$ is timelike, null, spacelike or causal according to the sign
of $\eta(v,v)$ as in [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]; in
particular the zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike and hence is
not causal, and the causal vectors are exactly the nonzero elements of
$\overline{C^+}\cup\overline{C^-}$.

**The closed cones and their boundaries.** By
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] the sets
$\overline{C^+}$ and $\overline{C^-}$ are convex cones with
$\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$. By
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]], applied in an
$\eta$-orthonormal basis whose first vector lies in $C^+$, the closure of the
component $\{v:v^0>|v_s|\}$ of the timelike set is
$\{v:v^0\ge|v_s|\}$ with boundary points exactly $0$ and the nonzero null
vectors of $\overline{C^+}$. Writing $N^+$ and $N^-$ for the sets of nonzero
future and past null vectors ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]),
this gives

$$\overline{C^+}=C^+\cup N^+\cup\{0\},\qquad \overline{C^-}=C^-\cup N^-\cup\{0\}.$$

**The objects fixed by this definition.**

**(a) Causal and chronological reachability.** For events $p,q\in A$ set
$p\le q$ if and only if $q-p\in\overline{C^+}$, and $p<q$ if and only if
$q-p\in C^+$. The first relation is read "$q$ is causally reachable from $p$"
and the second "$q$ is strictly (chronologically) reachable from $p$"; both are
relations on the set of events, and neither is asserted here to have any
property beyond being a relation.

**(b) Futures and pasts.** For an event $p\in A$ set

$$J^+(p):=\{q\in A:p\le q\}=p+\overline{C^+},\qquad I^+(p):=\{q\in A:p<q\}=p+C^+,$$

$$J^-(p):=\{q\in A:q\le p\}=p+\overline{C^-},\qquad I^-(p):=\{q\in A:q<p\}=p+C^-.$$

The displayed equalities hold because $q\in J^+(p)$ says exactly that the
displacement $q-p$ lies in $\overline{C^+}$, that is $q=p+v$ for some
$v\in\overline{C^+}$; here $p+v$ is the affine translation of
[[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]. Since $0\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}$
one has $p\in J^+(p)\cap J^-(p)$, and since $0$ is not timelike one has
$p\notin I^+(p)$ and $p\notin I^-(p)$. The sets
$J^\pm(p)$ and $I^\pm(p)$ are called the causal and chronological future and
past of $p$.

**(c) Causal diamonds.** For events $p,q\in A$ with $p\le q$, the causal diamond
of the ordered pair $(p,q)$ is the set

$$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)=\{r\in A:p\le r\le q\}.$$

The diamond is defined only under the hypothesis $p\le q$; some of its
properties are computed in the examples page of this pair.

**(d) Reachability by future causal paths.** A piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path is a piecewise $C^1$ curve $x:[a,b]\to A$ on a compact interval with
$a<b$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) all of
whose tangents are future causal: at every interior point of every open smooth
piece the tangent $x'(s)$ exists and is future causal, and at every partition
point of $[a,b]$ and at the endpoints $a$ and $b$ both one-sided
difference-quotient tangents that exist there exist and are future causal
vectors in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]. For events $p,q\in A$, say
that $q$ is reachable from $p$ by a future causal path when $p=q$, or when
$p\ne q$ and there are real numbers $a<b$ and a piecewise $C^1$ future causal
path $x:[a,b]\to A$ with $x(a)=p$ and $x(b)=q$. Write $R^+(p)$ for the set of
events reachable from $p$ in this sense; thus $p\in R^+(p)$ by the first clause.

**(e) Conventions and scope.** All objects above are defined from the affine
structure of $A$, the form $\eta$ and the time orientation alone: no chart, no
choice of origin, no spatial orientation of $V$ and no unit convention enters
their definition. This item asserts no property of these objects
beyond their being well-defined sets and relations: the reflexivity of $\le$ is
part of (b), while the transitivity of $\le$, the identification
$R^+(p)=J^+(p)$, the antisymmetry "$p\le q$ and $q\le p$ imply $p=q$", the
monotonicity of inertial coordinate time along future causal paths and the
invariance of these objects under proper orthochronous affine Lorentz maps are
proved later on this page and are not used here. No choice principle is used:
all objects are subsets or finite data built from a finite-dimensional real
vector space.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Adopt the postulates [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]],
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] and the causal signal restriction
[[post-sr-causal-signal-propagation]], and use the events, the relations $\le$
and $<$ and the sets $J^+$ and $I^+$ of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]] together with the
mathematical results
[[lem-sr-future-causal-sums-and-inertial-coordinate-criterion]],
[[lem-sr-spacelike-pairs-have-frame-dependent-time-order]] and
[[thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence]]. Let $x$ be the chart of
any inertial frame with $x^0=ct$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]). Then, as conditional
statements about the ideal model and not about any actual apparatus:

**(i) Receipt in the future light cone and absolute temporal order.** If a
signal is transmitted from $p$ to $q$, then $q\in J^+(p)$; if $q\ne p$, then
$x^0(q)>x^0(p)$ and $|x_s(q)-x_s(p)|\le x^0(q)-x^0(p)$ in every inertial chart,
and every inertial frame's time order places the reception after the emission.
Hence no inertial change of description reports the reception before the
emission, and the temporal order of the endpoints of a transmission is the same
in every inertial frame.

**(ii) Relay composition.** If signals are transmitted from $p$ to $q$ and from
$q$ to $r$, then $r\in J^+(p)$; if in addition $q\in I^+(p)$ or
$r\in I^+(q)$, then $r\in I^+(p)$. Thus relaying never leaves the causal future
of the first emission; a relay with at least one nonzero leg never returns to
the emission event.

**(iii) No closed signal loop.** If signals are transmitted from $p$ to $q$ and
from $q$ to $p$, then $p=q$. More generally, a finite chain of transmissions is closed if and
only if every leg has zero displacement; no nontrivial chain returns to its
own emission event.

**(iv) Frame independence of signal reachability.** For every proper
orthochronous affine Lorentz map $F$ of the model, which is an inertial change
of description by [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]], one has
$F(J^+(p))=J^+(F(p))$ and $F(I^+(p))=I^+(F(p))$ for all events $p$, and
$p\le q$ if and only if $F(p)\le F(q)$; hence whether the model admits a signal
between two events is the same in every inertial frame, in agreement with
[[pthm-sr-interval-and-cone-invariance]].

**(v) Spacelike pairs admit no signal.** If $q-p$ is spacelike, then no signal
is transmitted from $p$ to $q$, while there are inertial frames whose charts
assign $x^0(q)-x^0(p)$ either sign; consequently the model's signal restriction
is exactly the requirement that transmissions occur only between events whose
temporal order is observer-independent, with the emission the earlier endpoint.

**(vi) Scope and qualification.** Every clause is conditional on the adopted
postulates and is a statement about the ideal flat model; no actual signal,
transmitter, receiver, detector or measurement is described, no statistical or
empirical claim is made, and no inference from the model's structure to the
physical world is drawn. Clause (v) uses the mathematical fact
[[lem-sr-spacelike-pairs-have-frame-dependent-time-order]] and not an
experiment. No choice principle is used.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive power in the base and exponent is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes the origin; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Adopt the postulates of the spacetime-primitives page: the oriented
time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ as the spacetime of the
framework with the equations of the specified model covariant under proper
orthochronous affine Lorentz maps, which are the inertial changes of
description ([[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]), and the ideal clock and ideal
light assumptions, including that ideal vacuum light rays are the future null
straight lines and that inertial charts use $x^0=ct$
([[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]). Let $x$ and $x'$ be the
charts of any two inertial frames of the model. Then:

(i) the transition $x'\circ x^{-1}$ is an affine map $u\mapsto\Lambda u+b$
whose linear part $\Lambda$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix; in
particular for all events $p,q$ with coordinate differences
$\Delta=x(q)-x(p)$ and $\Delta'=x'(q)-x'(p)$ one has $\Delta'=\Lambda\Delta$
and $\eta_0(\Delta',\Delta')=\eta_0(\Delta,\Delta)$, where
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: the interval computed from the
coordinates of two events does not depend on the inertial chart used;

(ii) the causal classification of the displacement $q-p$ (timelike, null or
spacelike) and, for causal displacements, the relation "$q$ is in the future
of $p$" versus "$q$ is in the past of $p$" are independent of the inertial
chart used to compute them; likewise the sign of the interval
$I(p,q)=\eta(q-p,q-p)$ is chart-independent;

(iii) the class of future null straight lines is preserved by every inertial
transition: if a curve is a future null straight line in one inertial chart,
then its coordinate image in every other inertial chart is again a future null
straight line, and its coordinate speed computed as
$|\Delta x|/\Delta t$ equals $c$ in every inertial chart, consistently with
the light clause of [[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]];

(iv) the orientation and the oriented volume form of the model are invariant
under every inertial transition, and the composition of two inertial
transitions is again an inertial transition; for two transitions whose
relative parameters are $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ in a common spatial direction
the composed parameter is
$(\beta_1+\beta_2)/(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$.

**Scope and qualification.** This is a conditional statement about the adopted
model with ideal clocks, ideal light rays, flat classical spacetime and no
gravitational or quantum effects. It is not an empirical claim about nature,
it does not derive the postulates from experiment or from verbal symmetry
principles, and it inherits the idealizations of its premises; no measurement,
calibration or statistical inference is asserted.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and let $p,q\in A$ with $p\ne q$ and $q-p$
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Then:

**(a)** In the chart $x$ of every inertial frame the coordinate differences
$D:=x(q)-x(p)$ satisfy $|D^0|<|D_s|$, where $|D_s|$ is the Euclidean norm of the
spatial part $D_s:=(D^1,D^2,D^3)$ of $D$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]); in particular
$D_s\ne 0$.

**(b)** There is an inertial frame whose chart $x_0$ satisfies
$x_0^0(q)=x_0^0(p)$: the two events are simultaneous in that frame.

**(c)** There are inertial frames whose charts $x_+$ and $x_-$ satisfy
$x_+^0(q)>x_+^0(p)$ and $x_-^0(q)<x_-^0(p)$.

**(d) Explicit family.** Fix an inertial frame with chart $x$ and let
$e:=D_s/|D_s|$, so that $e$ is a unit spatial vector of that frame. For every
real number $b$ with $|b|<1$ let $B(be)$ be the passive boost of
[[def-lorentz-boost]] with parameter $be$, and let $x_b$ be the chart of the
inertial frame whose ordered basis is $e'_a:=B(be)^{-1}e_a$ and whose origin
event is the same event $o$. Then $x_b=B(be)\circ x$ (the linear map acting on
coordinate columns) and
$$x_b^0(q)-x_b^0(p)=\gamma_b\bigl(D^0-b|D_s|\bigr),\qquad \gamma_b:=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}.$$
This number is positive for $b<D^0/|D_s|$, zero for $b=D^0/|D_s|$ and negative
for $b>D^0/|D_s|$; since $-1<D^0/|D_s|<1$ by (a), all three cases occur among
values $|b|<1$, and the family $b\mapsto x_b$ depends continuously on $b$.

**(e) Scope.** The lemma concerns the inertial charts of the model;
"simultaneous in the frame" means equality of the frame's time coordinate
$x^0$, and no synchronization procedure, observer convention or physical
identification is asserted. No choice principle is used.

Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework the following restriction on
signal transmission, called the **causal signal restriction of the model**.

**(i) Causal restriction.** Let $p$ and $q$ be the emission and reception
events of an idealized transmission that carries a signal, where a *signal* is
understood as information, or a physical marker by which a prepared operation
at the emission event is correlated with an observation at the reception event,
within the model. Then the model admits such a transmission only if $q$ lies in
the causal future $J^+(p)$ of $p$
([[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]]), that is, only if
the displacement $q-p$ is zero or future causal
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]],
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]); equivalently, no signal
connects an event with an event outside its closed future light cone.

**(ii) Ideal light.** The ideal vacuum light signals of
[[post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light]] are the null boundary case of the
restriction: their displacement between emission and reception is future null,
so in the chart of every inertial frame with $x^0=ct$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]],
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]) they attain
$|x_s(q)-x_s(p)|=x^0(q)-x^0(p)$.

**(iii) Status.** This is an adopted assumption about the idealized model; it is
not a theorem of the affine geometry of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], it is
not derived here from the other postulates or from any experiment, and it is not
an empirical claim about nature. In particular the framework does not assert
that no physical process whatsoever exceeds $c$, and the question whether any
specified physical process is a signal of this model, and with what reliability
and reach, is left to a separate experimental interface.

**(iv) Explicit non-restriction.** The assumption does not forbid kinematic
patterns in which spacelike-separated events are produced by independent
prearranged mechanisms without any signal or energy transfer between them (for
example a prearranged row of devices triggered in a fixed sequence), and it
imposes no bound on correlations between spacelike-separated events.

**(v) Scope.** The assumption concerns idealized point-like transmission events
in the flat classical model and carries no statistical, apparatus, source or
detector content; no choice principle is used.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the special-relativity framework the following
two statements.

**(i) Spacetime.** The oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] is the spacetime of the
framework. Its points represent idealized physical events; the displacement
$q-p$ of two events represents an idealized spacetime separation of those
events; and the sign of $\eta(q-p,q-p)$ plus the chosen component $C^+$ is the
adopted causal structure: the timelike, null, spacelike, future-causal and
past-causal classifications of displacements are those of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]].

**(ii) Inertial changes of description.** Write $F:A\to A$ for a map for which
there is a linear map $L:V\to V$ satisfying

$$F(q)-F(p)=L(q-p)\qquad\text{for all }p,q\in A .$$

Such an $L$ is unique when it exists: for each $v\in V$ and any fixed $p\in A$,
applying the display to the pair $(p,p+v)$ gives $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$, so the value
$Lv$ is determined by $F$. An **inertial change of description** is such a map
$F$ whose linear part $L$ satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\quad\text{for all }v,w\in V,\qquad \det L=+1\ \text{relative to the fixed orientation of }V,\qquad L(C^+)=C^+ .$$

Adopt the assumption that the equations of the specific mechanical and
electromagnetic models developed from this framework are covariant under the
inertial changes of description: each such model equation has the same form
when its events are relabelled by $F$ and its displacements and other tensors
are transformed by $L$.

(iv) Every $L\in SO^+(V,\eta)$ preserves the interval $\eta(v,v)$, the causal
classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the
orientation, and the oriented volume form of the model:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,Lv_1,Lv_2,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$

derivations.claim: Work in the chart $x$ and write $t_1:=t(B_1)$. The outgoing signal is the ray $x^1=ut$ starting at $A_0$ (hypothesis S1 in the frame of $A$, whose chart is $x$), and $B$'s worldline is $x^1=L+vt$, so $ut_1=L+vt_1$, that is $t_1=L/(u-v)>0$ because $u>v$, and $x^1(B_1)=ut_1=uL/(u-v)>0$. The displacement $B_1-A_0$ has coordinates $(ct_1,ut_1,0,0)$, so $\eta=(u^2-c^2)t_1^2>0$ by [L2] and it is spacelike; this is (a).

Let $x'=B(v/c)\circ x$ be the chart of $B$'s rest frame, which is an inertial chart by [L5]; in it $B$ has constant spatial coordinate because $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0)=\gamma(L+vt-vt)=\gamma L$, and the return signal of S1-S2 moves in the $-x'^1$ direction at coordinate speed $u$, so its displacement in $x'$ is $(c\,\Delta t',-u\,\Delta t')$ for the positive coordinate-time increment $\Delta t'>0$ of the leg.

Transforming the displacement of step 2.1 back to $x$ with the inverse formulas of [L5] gives $c\,\Delta t=\gamma(c\,\Delta t'+\frac{v}{c}(-u\Delta t'))=\gamma c\,\Delta t'(1-vu/c^2)$ and the spatial displacement $\gamma(-u\Delta t'+\frac{v}{c}c\,\Delta t')=\gamma\Delta t'(v-u)$. The arrival event lies on $A$'s worldline $x^1=0$, so $\gamma\Delta t'(v-u)=-x^1(B_1)$, that is $\Delta t'=x^1(B_1)/(\gamma(u-v))>0$; substituting and using $x^1(B_1)=ut_1$ gives $\Delta t=x^1(B_1)(1-vu/c^2)/(u-v)$, which is negative exactly when $v>c^2/u$; the hypothesis $v>2u/(1+u^2/c^2)$ implies $v>c^2/u$, because $c^2/u<2u/(1+u^2/c^2)$ is equivalent to $u^2>c^2$. Hence $\Delta t<0$, and $t(A_1)=t(B_1)+\Delta t=\frac{L}{u-v}+\frac{uL(1-vu/c^2)}{(u-v)^2}=\frac{L(2u-v-vu^2/c^2)}{(u-v)^2}$, which is negative exactly when $v>2u/(1+u^2/c^2)$, as assumed; this is (b).

The arrival displacement is $A_1-A_0=(ct(A_1),0,0,0)$ with $t(A_1)<0$, so $\eta=-c^2t(A_1)^2<0$ with negative time coordinate: it is past timelike by [L2], and the reversed displacement $A_0-A_1=(c|t(A_1)|,0,0,0)$ satisfies $c|t(A_1)|>0=|D_s|$, so $A_0\in I^+(A_1)$, that is $A_1\in I^-(A_0)$, by [L1]. The return displacement $A_1-B_1$ has, in the chart $x'$ of step 2.1, the form $(c\Delta t',-u\Delta t')$ with $\eta'=(u^2-c^2)\Delta t'^2>0$, so it is spacelike there and, by the invariance of the interval under the Lorentz transition of [L6], spacelike in $x$ as well; this is (c).

Suppose the causal signal restriction holds for this configuration. The two legs are transmissions of the model, so [L4] applies to the chain $A_0\to B_1$ and $B_1\to A_1$ and gives $A_1\in J^+(A_0)$, that is $A_1-A_0\in\overline{C^+}$; by step 4.1, however, $A_1\in I^-(A_0)$, that is $A_0-A_1\in C^+$. Then $A_0-A_1\in C^+\subset\overline{C^+}$ and its negative $A_1-A_0\in\overline{C^+}$, so $A_0-A_1\in\overline{C^+}\cap\overline{C^-}=\{0\}$ by [L1], contradicting $A_0\ne A_1$ (their time coordinates differ) and $0\notin C^+$. Independently, the first leg is spacelike by step 1.1, so its reception $B_1$ does not lie in $J^+(A_0)$ by [L1], already violating the restriction's requirement. Hence the model S1-S4 and the causal signal restriction cannot both hold of one and the same process family; this is (d).

Everything above is a conditional computation inside S1-S4 in the ideal flat model: no observation is reported, nothing is asserted about the existence of superluminal transmitters, receivers, particles or signals, and the argument is void for patterns that transfer no signal or energy between their spacelike-separated events, for which by [L7] inertial charts of simultaneity and of either time order exist, so that the "speed $u$" of a leg is a chart-dependent description and not a frame-independent property; no quantum, gravitational, medium or detector effect, no phase or group velocity and no statistical or empirical claim is involved, and no choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
In every oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ and for
every event $o\in A$ there exists an inertial frame with origin $o$; consequently
inertial charts are defined at every event. Explicitly: start from any
$\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis $(f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3)$ of $V$; if $f_0$ is not in
$C^+$ then replacing $f_0$ by $-f_0$ makes the first vector future, because the
timelike set is the disjoint union of $C^+$ and $C^-$ and
$\eta(-f_0,-f_0)=\eta(f_0,f_0)$; the resulting ordered basis has some orientation
class, and if that class is not the positive class selected by the fixed
orientation of $V$, then replacing $e_1$ by $-e_1$ (or interchanging $e_1$ and
$e_2$) produces a positively oriented ordered basis, without destroying
$\eta$-orthonormality and without changing the first, future vector.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c, d \in F$.

1. **Translation invariance.** If $a < b$ then $a + c < b + c$.
2. **Adding inequalities.** If $a < b$ and $c < d$ then $a + c < b + d$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

derivations.claim: Fix an event $o\in A$ and an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with its basis and chart, and write $v=v^0e_0+v_s$, $w=w^0e_0+w_s$ with spatial parts $v_s,w_s\in S$; the coordinates are unique by [F1] and the spatial parts lie in $S$ by the definition of $S$ in [F3].

Since $v$ and $w$ are future timelike, [F2] gives $v^0>|v_s|$ and $w^0>|w_s|$; as $|v_s|,|w_s|\ge0$ by [F3], this yields $v^0>0$, $w^0>0$, and by strict monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives $(v^0)^2>|v_s|^2$ and $(w^0)^2>|w_s|^2$, so $a^2=(v^0)^2-|v_s|^2>0$ and $b^2=(w^0)^2-|w_s|^2>0$, whence $a=\sqrt{(v^0)^2-|v_s|^2}>0$ and $b=\sqrt{(w^0)^2-|w_s|^2}>0$ by uniqueness of the nonnegative root.

By bilinearity [F3], $-\eta(v,w)=v^0w^0-\delta(v_s,w_s)$; applying the finite Cauchy-Schwarz inequality [L4] to the coordinates of $v_s$ and $w_s$ in the $\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ gives $|\delta(v_s,w_s)|\le|v_s|\,|w_s|$, hence $\delta(v_s,w_s)\le|v_s|\,|w_s|$ and $-\eta(v,w)\ge x$ for $x:=v^0w^0-|v_s|\,|w_s|$.

The algebraic identity $x^2-\big((v^0)^2-|v_s|^2\big)\big((w^0)^2-|w_s|^2\big)=\big(v^0|w_s|-w^0|v_s|\big)^2\ge0$ holds by expansion, so $x^2\ge a^2b^2$; moreover $x=w^0\,(v^0-|v_s|)+|v_s|\,(w^0-|w_s|)$ is a sum of a positive real and a nonnegative real, so $x>0$ and in particular $x\ge0$.

Since $x\ge0$ and $ab>0$ with $x^2\ge(ab)^2$, monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives [L5] gives $x\ge ab$, and with step 2.2 this yields $-\eta(v,w)\ge ab>0$, which is (i); equivalently $\eta(v,w)\le-ab<0$.

Assume now $-\eta(v,w)=ab$. Then the chain $ab=-\eta(v,w)\ge x\ge ab$ of steps 2.2 and 4.1 is equality at both places, so $\delta(v_s,w_s)=|v_s|\,|w_s|$, and from $x=ab$ and the identity of step 3.1 we get $\big(v^0|w_s|-w^0|v_s|\big)^2=x^2-(ab)^2=0$, that is $v^0|w_s|=w^0|v_s|$.

Case $v_s=0$: then $v^0|w_s|=w^0|v_s|=0$ by step 5.1, and $v^0>0$, so $|w_s|=0$ and hence $w_s=0$; therefore $v=v^0e_0$ and $w=w^0e_0$ with $v^0,w^0>0$, and $v=(v^0/w^0)w$ exhibits $v$ as a positive multiple of $w$.
Case $w_s=0$: symmetrically $w^0|v_s|=v^0|w_s|=0$ with $w^0>0$ gives $v_s=0$, and $v^0>0$ gives $w=(w^0/v^0)v$, so $w$ is a positive multiple of $v$.

Case $v_s
eq0$ and $w_s
eq0$: the equality $\delta(v_s,w_s)=|v_s|\,|w_s|>0$ of step 5.1 is the equality case of the finite Cauchy-Schwarz inequality [L4] for two nonzero lists, so there are reals $(\lambda,\mu)
eq(0,0)$ with $\lambda v_s=\mu w_s$; here $\lambda
eq0$ (otherwise $w_s=0$) and $\mu
eq0$ (otherwise $v_s=0$), so $v_s=cw_s$ with $c:=\mu/\lambda$, and then $\delta(v_s,w_s)=c\,|w_s|^2$ while $|v_s|=|c|\,|w_s|$, so $c\,|w_s|^2=|c|\,|w_s|^2$ with $|w_s|^2=\delta(w_s,w_s)>0$; hence $c=|c|\ge0$, and $c>0$ because $c\,|w_s|^2=|v_s|\,|w_s|>0$; finally $v^0|w_s|=w^0|v_s|=w^0c|w_s|$ with $|w_s|>0$ gives $v^0=cw^0$, so $v=v^0e_0+cw_s=c\,(w^0e_0+w_s)=cw$ with $c>0$.
The three cases of steps 6.1-6.3 exhaust the possibilities, so equality $-\eta(v,w)=ab$ forces $v$ and $w$ to be positive proportional; this is the forward implication of (ii).

Conversely, if $v=tw$ with $t>0$, then bilinearity gives $-\eta(v,w)=-t\,\eta(w,w)=tb^2$ and $-\eta(v,v)=-t^2\eta(w,w)=t^2b^2$, so $a=tb$ by uniqueness of the nonnegative square root, whence $-\eta(v,w)=tb\cdot b=ab$; the case $w=tv$ is identical, and together with step 7.1 this proves (ii).
For (iii): if $v$ and $w$ are not positive proportional then equality fails by (ii), so $-\eta(v,w)>ab$ by step 4.1, while $\eta(v,w)<0$ holds in every case again by step 4.1.

For (iv): if $v,w$ are past timelike then $-v,-w$ are future timelike by [F2], with $-\eta(-v,-v)=-\eta(v,v)$, $-\eta(-w,-w)=-\eta(w,w)$ and $\eta(-v,-w)=\eta(v,w)$ by bilinearity [F3]; steps 4.1, 7.1 and 8.1 applied to $-v,-w$ therefore give $-\eta(v,w)=-\eta(-v,-w)\ge ab$, with equality exactly when $-v,-w$ are positive proportional, that is exactly when $v,w$ are positive proportional.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto M(u+x(o'))$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with causal terminology as in
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]], and let

$$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$$

be its **timelike set**. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] the
set $T$ has exactly two connected components, and each of them is nonempty,
open, convex and path-connected. A **time orientation** of $(V,\eta)$ is a
choice of one of these two components. Fixing such a choice, write $C^+$ for the
chosen component and

$$C^-:=T\setminus C^+$$

for the other component; thus $T=C^+\sqcup C^-$ is a disjoint union and
$C^+$, $C^-$ are exactly the two components supplied by the lemma. Relative to
this choice a vector $v\in V$ is

- **future timelike** when $v\in C^+$;
- **past timelike** when $v\in C^-$;
- **future null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$;
- **past null** when $v\neq 0$, $\eta(v,v)=0$ and $v\in\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$;
- **future causal** when it is future timelike or future null;
- **past causal** when it is past timelike or past null.

The sets $\operatorname{cl}(C^+)$ and $\operatorname{cl}(C^-)$ are the
**future closed cone** and the **past closed cone** of the time-oriented space
$(V,\eta,C^+)$. By [[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]] each of them
is a convex cone, their intersection is $\{0\}$, and a vector is causal exactly
when it is future causal or past causal, in which case exactly one of these two
alternatives holds: no nonzero vector is both future causal and past causal.
The timelike vectors are exactly the points of $T=C^+\cup C^-$, and
$0\notin T$ because $\eta(0,0)=0$; since a null vector is nonzero with
$\eta(v,v)=0$, no vector is both timelike and null, so the classes above are
mutually exclusive where the definitions say they are: no vector is both future
and past causal, and no timelike vector is null.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes $\delta$ and $\times$. The only
$\eta$-invariant structure of the model remains $\eta$; the Euclidean spatial
structure is not an additional invariant of $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and
let $v,w\in V$ be future timelike vectors. Put
$a:=\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}>0$ and $b:=\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}>0$, the timelike lengths of
$v$ and $w$. Then:

**(i)** $-\eta(v,w)\ge ab>0$.

**(ii)** Equality $-\eta(v,w)=ab$ holds if and only if $v$ and $w$ are
positive proportional, that is $w=tv$ for some real $t>0$, or $v=tw$ for some
real $t>0$.

**(iii)** Consequently $-\eta(v,w)>ab$ whenever $v$ and $w$ are not positive
proportional, and $\eta(v,w)<0$ in every case.

**(iv)** For two past timelike vectors $v,w$ the same inequality
$-\eta(v,w)\ge\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$ holds, with equality if and
only if they are positive proportional, because $-v$ and $-w$ are future
timelike and $\eta(-v,-w)=\eta(v,w)$.

The statement uses only $\eta$ and the future cone $C^+$ and involves no chart,
frame or choice principle.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c, d \in F$.

1. **Translation invariance.** If $a < b$ then $a + c < b + c$.
2. **Adding inequalities.** If $a < b$ and $c < d$ then $a + c < b + d$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Fix an event $o\in A$ and an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with its coordinates; by [F1] every vector $u$ is written uniquely as $u=u^0e_0+u_s$ with $u_s\in S$, the pairing is $\eta(u,u')=-u^0u'^0+\delta(u_s,u'_s)$, and $u\in C^+\iff u^0>|u_s|$.

Let $v,w$ be future timelike. Then $(v+w)^0=v^0+w^0>|v_s|+|w_s|\ge|v_s+w_s|=|(v+w)_s|$: the first inequality adds the two strict inequalities $v^0>|v_s|$ and $w^0>|w_s|$ that [F1] gives from future timelikeness, the second is the triangle inequality of the spatial norm, and the displayed equalities are additivity of coordinates; hence $v+w$ is future timelike.

Let $a:=\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$, $b:=\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$ and $C:=\sqrt{-\eta(v+w,v+w)}$, which is a positive real by step 2.1; bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$ give $C^2=-\eta(v+w,v+w)=-\eta(v,v)-2\eta(v,w)-\eta(w,w)=a^2+b^2+2\,(-\eta(v,w))$, and $-\eta(v,w)\ge ab$ by the reversed Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, so multiplying by the positive number $2$ and adding the constant $a^2+b^2$ yields $C^2\ge a^2+b^2+2ab=(a+b)^2$.

For $t\in(0,1)$ the vectors $tv$ and $(1-t)w$ are future timelike: $(tv)^0=tv^0>t|v_s|=|tv_s|$ because $t>0$ preserves the strict inequality and $|tv_s|=t|v_s|$ by the coordinate formula $|z|=\sqrt{(z^1)^2+(z^2)^2+(z^3)^2}$ of [F2] together with uniqueness of the nonnegative root, and symmetrically $(1-t)w^0>(1-t)|w_s|=|(1-t)w_s|$; for $t=0$ and $t=1$ the vector $tv+(1-t)w$ equals $w$ respectively $v$, which are future timelike.

For the base case $k=1$ of (c): a future timelike vector $v_1$ is its own sum, $\sqrt{-\eta(v_1,v_1)}\ge\sqrt{-\eta(v_1,v_1)}$ holds with equality, and $v_1=1\cdot v_1$ exhibits $v_1$ as a positive multiple of the single future timelike vector $u:=v_1$, so the equality characterization of (c) is satisfied for $k=1$.
Since $C\ge0$ and $a+b\ge0$ with $C^2\ge(a+b)^2$, monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives [L4] gives $C\ge a+b$: this is the inequality of (a).

For $t\in(0,1)$, (a) applied to the future timelike vectors $tv$ and $(1-t)w$ of step 3.2 gives $tv+(1-t)w$ future timelike and $\sqrt{-\eta(tv+(1-t)w,tv+(1-t)w)}\ge\sqrt{-\eta(tv,tv)}+\sqrt{-\eta((1-t)w,(1-t)w)}=t\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}+(1-t)\sqrt{-\eta(w,w)}$, the two displayed equalities using bilinearity and uniqueness of the nonnegative root; this is the inequality of (b) on the open interval.

Equality holds in (a) if and only if $C=a+b$, which by monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives [L4] is equivalent to $C^2=(a+b)^2$, hence, subtracting the common term $a^2+b^2$ from the two displays of step 3.1 and multiplying by $1/2$, to $-\eta(v,w)=ab$, and by the equality case of the reversed Cauchy-Schwarz inequality [F3] to $v$ and $w$ being positive proportional; this proves (a).

Induction step, membership and inequality: assume $k\ge1$ and that the claim of (c) holds for the integer $k$; let $v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}$ be future timelike and put $s:=v_1+\cdots+v_k$, which is future timelike by the induction hypothesis; applying (a) of steps 2.1 and 4.1 to the future timelike vectors $s$ and $v_{k+1}$ gives $s+v_{k+1}=v_1+\cdots+v_{k+1}$ future timelike and $\sqrt{-\eta(s+v_{k+1},s+v_{k+1})}\ge\sqrt{-\eta(s,s)}+\sqrt{-\eta(v_{k+1},v_{k+1})}\ge\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sqrt{-\eta(v_i,v_i)}+\sqrt{-\eta(v_{k+1},v_{k+1})}$, the second inequality being the induction hypothesis.

Equality in the interior inequality of (b) for $0<t<1$ holds if and only if $tv$ and $(1-t)w$ are positive proportional, by the equality case of (a) established in step 5.1 applied to the interior inequality of (b) of step 4.2; since $t>0$ and $1-t>0$, this is equivalent to $v$ and $w$ being positive proportional; at $t=0$ and $t=1$ the inequality reduces to an identity $b\ge b$ or $a\ge a$, and the statement makes no interior equality claim there, so (b) is proved.

Induction step, equality characterization: with the notation of step 5.2, if equality holds for the $k+1$ vectors, then both inequalities in the chain of step 5.2 are equalities; the second equality means that the equality case of the induction hypothesis applies to $v_1,\dots,v_k$, so there are a future timelike $u$ and reals $c_1,\dots,c_k>0$ with $v_i=c_iu$ and $s=(\sum_{i=1}^kc_i)u$; the first equality is the equality case of (a) for $s$ and $v_{k+1}$, so $s$ and $v_{k+1}$ are positive proportional, and since $s\neq0$ this gives $v_{k+1}=c_{k+1}u$ for some real $c_{k+1}>0$, so all $k+1$ vectors are positive multiples of the single future timelike vector $u$; conversely, if $v_i=c_iu$ with $c_i>0$ and $u$ future timelike for $i=1,\dots,k+1$, then $v_1+\cdots+v_{k+1}=(\sum_ic_i)u$ and bilinearity with uniqueness of the nonnegative root give $\sqrt{-\eta(\sum_iv_i,\sum_iv_i)}=(\sum_ic_i)\sqrt{-\eta(u,u)}=\sum_i\sqrt{-\eta(v_i,v_i)}$, so equality holds.

By [L6], applied to the property "$v_1,\dots,v_k$ future timelike implies the conclusions of (c) for these vectors", the base case of step 3.3 and the induction steps 5.2 and 6.2 prove (c) for every integer $k\ge1$: membership and inequality from step 5.2, and the equality characterization from step 6.2.
